summary.text: Take \(n=23492890653051=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\), whose five displayed factors are prime. Since the gcd-sum is multiplicative on coprime inputs and equals \(2p-1\) at a prime \(p\), it is \(610815156979325=26n-1\) here, so \(\gcd(n,1+\sum_{k=1}^n\gcd(k,n))=n\) and the quotient is \(1\), although \(n\) is composite (indeed divisible by \(3\)).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n \gcd(k,n),
\qquad
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+S(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit a composite integer \(N\) for which \(S(N)=26N-1\). It will then follow immediately that \(a(N)=1\).

First we establish the form of the gcd-sum that will be used in the calculation. For each divisor \(d\mid n\), the integers \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq n\) and \(\gcd(k,n)=d\) are precisely the integers \(k=dj\) such that
\[
1\leq j\leq n/d,\qquad \gcd(j,n/d)=1.
\]
There are \(\varphi(n/d)\) such integers. Thus
\[
S(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d). \tag{1}
\]
This also shows that \(S\) is multiplicative. Indeed, if \(\gcd(m,n)=1\), each divisor of \(mn\) has a unique form \(d_1d_2\), with \(d_1\mid m\) and \(d_2\mid n\). Moreover, the two factors \(m/d_1\) and \(n/d_2\) are coprime, so Euler's totient is multiplicative on them. Consequently, using (1),
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(mn)
&=\sum_{d_1\mid m}\sum_{d_2\mid n}
 d_1d_2\,\varphi\!\left(\frac{m}{d_1}\frac{n}{d_2}\right)\\
&=\left(\sum_{d_1\mid m}d_1\varphi(m/d_1)\right)
  \left(\sum_{d_2\mid n}d_2\varphi(n/d_2)\right)\\
&=S(m)S(n). \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
For a prime \(p\), its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\), and hence
\[
S(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1. \tag{3}
\]

Now consider
\[
N=23492890653051
  =3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341. \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, we justify that all five factors displayed here are distinct primes. Primality of \(3,37,43\) follows immediately by trial division by primes no greater than their square roots. The two larger primality assertions can be checked compactly by the following elementary order criterion.

Suppose that the complete prime factorization of \(M-1\) is known, and that an integer \(b\) satisfies
\[
b^{M-1}\equiv1\pmod M
\]
and, for every distinct prime \(q\mid M-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(M-1)/q}-1,M\bigr)=1. \tag{5}
\]
Then \(M\) is prime. To see this, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(M\), and let \(t\) be the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(r\). The first congruence gives \(t\mid M-1\). Condition (5) says that, for every prime \(q\mid M-1\), the order \(t\) does not divide \((M-1)/q\). Therefore \(t\) contains the full power of every prime occurring in \(M-1\), and so \(t=M-1\). On the other hand, the order of a nonzero residue modulo the prime \(r\) divides \(r-1\). Hence \(M-1\mid r-1\), so \(r\geq M\). Since \(r\mid M\), this forces \(r=M\), proving that \(M\) is prime.

For \(M=42307\), we have the complete factorization
\[
M-1=42306=2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641.
\]
The number \(641\) is prime: since \(\sqrt{641}<26\), it suffices to test the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\), and none divides \(641\). (The corresponding nonzero remainders are immediate; for the primes from \(7\) onward they are respectively \(4,3,4,12,14,20\).) With \(b=3\), repeated squaring gives
\[
3^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&(42306)/q&3^{42306/q}\pmod{42307}\\ \hline
2&21153&42306\\
3&14102&36715\\
11&3846&17937\\
641&66&10961
\end{array}
\]
The required gcds are all \(1\). Explicit Bézout identities certifying this are
\[
\begin{aligned}
21153(42305)-21152(42307)&=1,\\
-12239(36714)+10621(42307)&=1,\\
6088(17936)-2581(42307)&=1,\\
-6651(10960)+1723(42307)&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here each first argument, namely \(42305,36714,17936,10960\), is one less than the residue in the corresponding row. Thus the order criterion proves that \(42307\) is prime.

Similarly,
\[
116341-1=116340=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
The number \(277\) is prime: \(\sqrt{277}<17\), and trial division by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) gives no divisor. With \(b=14\), repeated squaring gives
\[
14^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&116340/q&14^{116340/q}\pmod{116341}\\ \hline
2&58170&116340\\
3&38780&50801\\
5&23268&81650\\
7&16620&10889\\
277&420&35125
\end{array}
\]
Again the relevant gcds are \(1\), as witnessed by
\[
\begin{aligned}
58170(116339)-58169(116341)&=1,\\
21846(50800)-9539(116341)&=1,\\
-15490(81649)+10871(116341)&=1,\\
-9200(10888)+861(116341)&=1,\\
-9026(35124)+2725(116341)&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The order criterion therefore proves that \(116341\) is prime as well. This completes the justification that the factors in (4) are distinct primes. Their product can be checked successively as
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\quad111\cdot43=4773,
\quad4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\quad201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051.
\]

Because the five prime factors in (4) are pairwise coprime, multiplicativity (2) and the prime formula (3) now give
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(N)
&=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
  (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
&=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The successive products are
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\quad365\cdot85=31025,
\quad31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
and
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
Thus
\[
S(N)=610815156979325.
\]
But direct multiplication also gives
\[
26N-1
=26\cdot23492890653051-1
=610815156979325.
\]
Therefore
\[
1+S(N)=26N.
\]
It follows that
\[
\gcd(N,1+S(N))=\gcd(N,26N)=N,
\]
and hence
\[
a(N)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,1+S(N))}=\frac NN=1. \tag{6}
\]

Finally, \(N\neq1\), and \(N\) is not prime: equation (4) exhibits \(3\) as a divisor, with \(1<3<N\). Thus (6) gives a composite integer other than \(1\) at which \(a(N)=1\). This contradicts the claimed implication that \(a(n)=1\) only when \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime, and therefore disproves the stated conjecture.
